title: Reform begins
hook: German Jews change services: sermons, organs, the vernacular

segments.voice: Yesterday, Napoleon's Sanhedrin: the law of the kingdom is the law, and a careful line drawn with it. Your line was loyal questions. Where did your yes end? Today, Jews in Germany ask a different question, about their own synagogues. Day nine hundred seventy-five.

A Sabbath morning in a German town. The Jewish families walk in to pray, and the room sounds different. There is an organ. A choir sings. Some of the prayers are in German, the language these families now speak at home and at work. And then a man stands up and gives a sermon, in German, polished and earnest. Some in the room are moved to tears; for once they understand every word. Others walk out shaken; to them this is no longer the synagogue of their parents. Today, Reform begins.
screen: `AN ORGAN, A CHOIR.` → `PRAYERS IN GERMAN.` → `TEARS, AND PEOPLE WALKING OUT.`

segments.voice: The new citizens of yesterday's story faced a real worry. Their children were learning German, going to German schools, entering German professions. And some of them were drifting away from Judaism altogether, finding the synagogue long, hard to follow, and out of step with the life they lived the rest of the week. A group of German Jews decided the answer was to change the service itself. A layman named Israel Jacobson built a house of prayer with an organ and held services with German hymns and German sermons. In Hamburg, a congregation opened a temple with its own new prayer book, shorter, partly in German, and with changes to some prayers about the return to Zion. They wanted worship that was dignified, understandable, and modern. The organ became a symbol of the whole fight. Supporters could point to the Psalms. Here is a line of Psalm one hundred fifty, as the King James Bible renders it: "Praise him with stringed instruments and organs." Opponents answered that playing an instrument on the Sabbath breaks the Sabbath, that the organ imitated the church, and that the prayers were not anyone's to rewrite. Traditional rabbis published rulings against the Hamburg prayer book. The reformers feared losing the young to the world. The traditionalists feared losing the prayers their parents had said, word for word. The Reform movement grew out of these first changes, and so did new ways of defending tradition, which we'll meet tomorrow. And the question the organ raised, what may change in a service and who gets to decide, would be argued in synagogue after synagogue.
screen: `CHILDREN DRIFTING AWAY.` · `ORGAN, CHOIR, GERMAN SERMONS.` · `PRAISE HIM WITH ORGANS?` · then, large: `TWO FEARS, ONE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: notice one change you've lived through. Sit comfortably and breathe out slowly. Think of something that changed around you: a family tradition done a new way, a community that modernized, a job that went digital, a holiday that looks different now than when you were small. Let yourself feel both sides. What was gained? What was lost? Who welcomed it, and who walked out quietly? You don't have to decide who was right. Just hold both the tears of the one who finally understood and the shock of the one who no longer recognized the room. The bell holds the time.
Jacobson. The layman who built the first Reform-style house of prayer, with an organ, German hymns, and sermons the young could understand. Today's word.
Your line: tears, and people walking out. Today, when you hear someone defend an old way or push a new one, listen for the fear underneath it. Day nine hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Reform synagogues today commonly hold services that mix Hebrew with the local language and include instrumental music, while Orthodox synagogues keep a traditional Hebrew service without instruments on Shabbat.
